CausalChain: Tumor stress (hypoxia/oxidative stress) -> Increased biogenesis of specific tRFs -> Selective packaging of tRFs into exosomes -> Exosome secretion into tumor microenvironment -> Uptake of exosomal tRFs by macrophages -> Binding of tRFs to key RNA-binding proteins in macrophages -> Altered gene expression leading to M2-like (immunosuppressive) polarization -> Enhanced tumor progression and metastasis
Hypothesis: Stress-induced tRNA-derived fragments are secreted via exosomes by cancer cells and, upon uptake by tumor-associated macrophages, reprogram these immune cells to adopt an immunosuppressive, pro-tumoral phenotype that drives tumor progression and metastasis.
Abstract: Recent studies have highlighted the multifaceted role of tRNA-derived fragments (tRFs) in regulating gene expression, protein translation, and the stress response, including in viral infections and cancer. Building on these findings, we propose that tRFs have a novel, extracellular signaling function in the tumor microenvironment. Specifically, under stress conditions, cancer cells may selectively package tRFs into exosomes. Once released, these exosomal tRFs can be taken up by tumor-associated immune cells, such as macrophages, altering their gene regulatory networks and driving a shift toward an immunosuppressive, pro-tumoral polarization state. This mechanism could provide a link between cellular stress responses and the modulation of the immune microenvironment, ultimately contributing to tumor progression and metastasis.
